cases.title: The First Revelation: Terror, Doubt, and a Christian Referee
cases.claim: By Islam's own most-trusted sources, Muhammad's first encounter with revelation left him terrified and unable to identify its source. In Aisha's long narration (Sahih al-Bukhari 3, repeated at Sahih al-Bukhari 6982), the being in the cave of Hira seized and squeezed him three times; he fled to Khadijah trembling, crying 'Cover me! Cover me!' and confessing, 'I fear that something may happen to me.' Ibn Ishaq's sirah — Islam's earliest biography — records his own first hypotheses as the worst available: 'ecstatic poet or a man possessed... Woe is me' (Guillaume, Life of Muhammad, p. 106). It took Khadijah and her cousin Waraqah bin Naufal — a Christian conversant with prior scripture — to pronounce the visitor divine. Bukhari 6982 then describes the fatra (pause in revelation) during which, 'as we have heard,' he grieved so deeply he repeatedly 'intended to throw himself from the tops of high mountains' — a line carried only in al-Zuhri's appended report, not Aisha's chain (see rationale). Contrast Isaiah 6, Jeremiah 1, and Luke 1: fear is present, but God self-identifies, and the angel's first word is 'Fear not.'

sources.name: Sahih al-Bukhari 6982 (sunnah.com)
Sahih al-Bukhari 3 (sunnah.com)
Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah (A. Guillaume translation)
Mahajjah — analysis of the mountain-peaks report
Islam365 — Did the Prophet contemplate suicide?

cases.response: Muslim scholars answer that terror is precisely what a genuine encounter with the transcendent produces — Moses fled from the sign at the bush (Quran 28:31) — and that fear argues sincerity: an impostor invents a flattering commissioning, not one that leaves him suspecting madness. The mountain-tops line, they stress, is not Aisha's testimony at all: Ibn Hajar (Fath al-Bari) identifies it as a balagh of al-Zuhri — introduced by 'fima balaghana' ('as we have heard'), transmitted only in Ma'mar's recension and absent from 'Uqayl's and Yunus's — a disconnected report carrying no sahih weight. Waraqah's role is read as providence: a scholar of previous revelation recognizing the same Namus (angel) who came to Moses, confirming continuity rather than supplying legitimacy Muhammad lacked.
cases.rationale: Graded admitted because every load-bearing fact sits in Islam's own canon and is undisputed as fact: the terror, 'Cover me,' 'I fear for myself,' and the need for Waraqah — a Christian — to certify the encounter as divine (Bukhari 3, 6982; Muslim 160). Honesty requires conceding the strongest Muslim point, and this site does: the suicidal-despair line is weak by Islam's own hadith science — al-Zuhri's unattributed addendum via Ma'mar only — so do not build the argument on it. Build it on what no one disputes: the recipient of the revelation could not himself identify its source, and the identification came from a human. Biblical commissioning scenes carry divine self-identification; Paul's warning in Galatians 1:8 about 'an angel from heaven' preaching another gospel frames the stakes. Severity high: the question 'how do you know it was Gabriel?' touches the foundation of everything downstream.

cases.title: Are Jews and Christians Saved? Quran 2:62 vs 3:85
cases.claim: Quran 2:62 promises that 'those who believed, and those who were Jews, and the Christians, and the Sabians — whoever believed in Allah and the Last Day and did righteousness — will have their reward with their Lord, and no fear will there be concerning them.' Quran 5:69 repeats the promise nearly verbatim. Yet Quran 3:85 declares: 'Whoever desires other than Islam as religion — never will it be accepted from him, and he, in the Hereafter, will be among the losers' (cf. 3:19). The classical resolution concedes the tension: al-Tabari's tafsir on 2:62 records Ibn Abbas saying the verse was abrogated (naskh) by 3:85 — though Mujahid and al-Dahhak held 2:62 muhkama (standing), and Tabari himself preferred a restricted reading. Sahih Muslim 153 seals the exclusivist position: any Jew or Christian who hears of Muhammad and dies without believing in his message 'will be among the inhabitants of the Fire.' Modern scholars split between abrogation and restriction (2:62 meant pre-Muhammad communities, or those who subsequently accept Islam). Either way, the plain reading of the two texts pulls in opposite directions — and the abrogation solution is itself an admission of it.

sources.name: Quran 2:62 (quran.com)
Quran 3:85 (quran.com)
Sahih Muslim 153 (sunnah.com)
Yaqeen Institute — Abrogated Rulings in the Qur'an
Answering Islam — Abrogated Verses of the Quran

cases.response: Most Muslim exegetes deny any contradiction. On the majority reading, 2:62 addresses Jews, Christians, and Sabians who lived faithfully before Muhammad, or who accept him once his message reaches them — 'whoever believed in Allah and the Last Day' is read as belief on Islam's own terms, which after 610 AD includes Muhammad's prophethood. Others note that when Ibn Abbas said 'naskh' he frequently meant takhsis (specification), not repeal — 3:85 clarifies the scope of 2:62 rather than cancelling a salvation once offered. On this view the verses teach one consistent doctrine across time: every era's believers must follow the prophet sent to them, and after Muhammad that means Islam. The Quran, they argue, elsewhere criticizes Jews and Christians precisely for failing their own covenants, so 2:62 was never a blanket pluralism.

responseSource.name: Yaqeen Institute — Abrogated Rulings in the Qur'an

cases.rationale: Graded contested, not unrefuted, because the restriction reading is a coherent harmonization the Arabic can bear, and it was held by classical authorities (Mujahid, al-Dahhak, arguably Tabari himself) — this site does not overclaim. But the argument retains real force: the harmonization must be imported, since nothing in 2:62's wording limits it to a past era; the abrogation report preserved in Islam's own premier tafsir concedes that the earliest readers felt the collision; and Sahih Muslim 153 makes the operative doctrine unambiguous. The evangelistic use is not 'gotcha' but clarity: a Muslim friend citing 2:62 as proof Islam honors Christians should know their own tradition denies that Christians who remain Christians are saved. Contrast the New Testament's single consistent claim (John 14:6, Acts 4:12) with a God 'with whom there is no variation' (James 1:17).

cases.title: Slavery: Regulated Forever, Abolished from Outside
cases.claim: Islamic law moralized slavery but never abolished it. The Quran makes captive women lawful to their captors — 'and [prohibited to you are] married women, except those your right hands possess' (Quran 4:24; cf. 33:50) — and while manumission is meritorious (Sahih al-Bukhari 2517) and contracts of emancipation encouraged (24:33), enslavement itself remained lawful in every classical school. Muhammad owned, bought, sold, and freed slaves per sahih sources: he bought a slave for two black slaves (Sahih Muslim 1602), took captives from Banu Mustaliq (Sahih al-Bukhari 2541), and held Mariyah the Copt as a concubine. No Muslim polity abolished slavery from within sharia: abolition came under Western and colonial pressure — Saudi Arabia in 1962, Oman in 1970, Mauritania in 1981 (the last country on earth; criminalized only in 2007, with anti-slavery organizations documenting continued practice). ISIS's 2014 revival of sexual slavery of Yazidi women (Dabiq issue 4, 'The Revival of Slavery Before the Hour') cited classical fiqh directly. The Mosaic law, by contrast, regulated an existing institution with release built in — sabbatical manumission (Exodus 21:2), a death penalty for man-stealing (Exodus 21:16), an anti-return law sheltering escaped slaves (Deuteronomy 23:15-16) — and the abolition movement itself was overwhelmingly Christian-led (Wilberforce, the Quakers).

sources.name: Quran 4:24 (quran.com)
Sahih Muslim 1602 (sunnah.com)
IslamQA 94840 — Slavery in Islam
Brandeis University — Islam and Slavery (Feminist Sexual Ethics Project)
CNN — Slavery's Last Stronghold (Mauritania)

cases.response: The Muslim defense is gradualism plus trajectory: Islam inherited a world economy built on slavery and uniquely channeled it toward emancipation — freeing slaves is prescribed expiation for broken oaths and other sins, a designated category of zakat spending (9:60), and among the most praised acts of piety; masters must feed and clothe slaves as themselves; the mukataba contract (24:33) let slaves purchase freedom. Muhammad freed slaves and elevated one, Zayd, to adopted-son status and army command. Contemporary scholars add that modern Muslim states' accession to abolition treaties is religiously binding, since treaty obligations are enforceable in sharia, and that the slave-raiding of groups like ISIS violates that binding consensus. On this account Islam's mechanism was emancipation-by-attrition, and abolition fulfills rather than contradicts its intent.
cases.rationale: Graded admitted because the core facts are conceded on all sides — including by IslamQA today, which affirms slavery was never prohibited by sharia. The trajectory defense explains amelioration but not the thirteen centuries in which no school and no state moved from amelioration to abolition, nor why abolition arrived only under external pressure, nor why ISIS could cite mainstream classical fiqh rather than fringe texts. Be honest about the Bible: Mosaic law also regulated slavery, and Christians long misused Scripture to defend it. The difference is direction — release provisions, the man-stealing capital law, Deuteronomy's shelter for escapees, Philemon's 'no longer as a slave but as a beloved brother,' and an abolition movement driven by Christian conviction. Use this comparison carefully and concede Christian failures first; the argument is strongest when it stays about the texts and legal systems, not about whose ancestors behaved better.

cases.title: Female Circumcision in Classical Fiqh: A Weak Hadith with a Long Shadow
cases.claim: Classical Islamic law addresses female circumcision, and one school mandated it. The Shafi'i manual Umdat al-Salik (Reliance of the Traveller, e4.3, certified by al-Azhar in its English edition) rules circumcision obligatory (wajib) for both sexes, describing the female form as cutting the prepuce of the clitoris — with translation disputes over whether the Arabic bazr means the prepuce or the clitoris itself. Hanbalis were split between obligatory and honorable; Hanafis and Malikis called it recommended or noble (makrumah), not required. IslamQA's current answer 60314 still defends the practice as 'part of the fitrah.' The main supporting hadith — Umm Atiyyah, told by Muhammad 'do not cut severely, as that is better for a woman and more desirable for a husband' (Sunan Abi Dawud 5271) — was declared weak by Abu Dawud himself ('not strong,' mursal), and by al-Iraqi and al-Azimabadi, though al-Albani later authenticated it via corroborating chains. Practice tracks madhhab geography (Shafi'i Southeast Asia, Egypt, Horn of Africa) — but the custom pre-dates Islam and exists among non-Muslims in those regions. The 2006 al-Azhar conference condemned FGM as criminal aggression, and Grand Mufti Ali Gomaa's 2007 fatwa forbade it.

sources.name: Reliance of the Traveller (Umdat al-Salik), e4.3
Sunan Abi Dawud 5271 (sunnah.com)
IslamQA 60314 — Circumcision of girls
Stop FGM Middle East — Fatwas against FGM
UNICEF Egypt — FGM summary

cases.response: Muslim scholars opposing the practice argue the case from inside the tradition: the Umm Atiyyah hadith is weak by the assessment of Abu Dawud himself, so no obligation can be built on it; nothing in the Quran addresses the practice at all; and the sharia's governing principle of la darar (no harm) forbids any procedure medicine shows to be injurious. The Fiqh Council of North America and Grand Mufti Ali Gomaa have ruled FGM prohibited outright; the 2006 al-Azhar conference called it punishable aggression. Defenders of the classical position, meanwhile, insist the fiqh only ever sanctioned a minimal symbolic cut — the 'do not cut severely' wording itself — and that severe forms (infibulation) are pre-Islamic African custom the jurists never endorsed, practiced by Christians and animists in the same regions.

responseSource.name: Fiqh Council of North America — Fatwa on female genital cutting

cases.rationale: Graded contested because the honest picture cuts both ways: the textual basis is weak (weak per Abu Dawud himself, no Quranic support), major Muslim authorities now prohibit the practice, and the custom is regional and pre-Islamic — yet it remains true that classical fiqh canonized rather than abolished it, one school made it obligatory, and IslamQA defends it today. State every one of those clauses or state none. Pastoral guidance, emphatically: this topic is explosive and almost always counterproductive in personal evangelism. It exists in this database for completeness and for the rare context where a Muslim friend has raised comparative women's-status arguments and expects candor in return. Never open with it; never use it as a weapon; lead with listening. A Muslim friend likely finds FGM as abhorrent as you do — treating them as its defender is both unjust and conversation-ending.

cases.title: Grammatical Irregularities in a Book Claiming Perfect Eloquence
cases.claim: The Quran stakes its central miracle on linguistic inimitability — 'produce a surah like it' (Quran 2:23) — in 'clear Arabic' (12:2). Yet classical scholars themselves catalogued grammatical anomalies. Quran 4:162 has al-muqimina ('those who establish prayer') in the accusative where the surrounding nouns are nominative; 5:69 has al-sabi'una in the nominative where the particle inna requires the accusative (contrast 2:62 and 22:17, where the same word is correctly declined); 20:63 reads inna hadhani la-sahirani, using the dual nominative hadhani where inna demands the accusative hadhayni; 2:177 puts al-sabirina in the accusative amid nominatives. Early reports acknowledge the problem: Uthman is said to have remarked of the compiled text, 'I see errors (lahn) in it, and the Arabs will correct them with their tongues,' and a report via Abu Ubayd's Fada'il al-Qur'an attributes to Aisha the judgment that 4:162, 5:69, and 20:63 are 'the fault of the scribes.' Both reports are themselves disputed — their chains are contested and Muslim scholars reject or reinterpret them. Classical grammarians harmonized each verse (poetic license, dialectal inna, praise-clause accusative), which is itself evidence the anomalies were felt.

sources.name: M. Rafiqul-Haqq & P. Newton — The Qur'an: Grammatical Errors
Islamic Awareness — Responses to grammatical errors in the Qur'an
Tulayhah — al-Suyuti on alleged grammatical errors
IslamQA 135752 — Reports attributing linguistic errors to the Qur'an
The Islam Issue — Scribal mistakes and variants in the Quran

cases.response: Muslim grammarians and modern academics answer that these constructions are attested classical Arabic, not errors: the accusative in 4:162 and 2:177 is the well-known qat' construction (specification for praise, 'and especially those who…'), documented in pre-Islamic poetry; 5:69's nominative can be a delayed-topic construction; and 20:63's hadhani matches the dialect of certain Arab tribes (attributed to Banu al-Harith) in which the dual retains the alif in all cases — a reading known to the earliest philologists. The Uthman and Aisha reports, they argue, are unreliable: their isnads are contested, lahn in early usage could mean recitation style rather than error, and it is historically implausible that Uthman would standardize a text he believed defective while companions who memorized the Quran raised no such objection. Standard grammars were codified after the Quran and partly from it.

responseSource.name: Islamic Awareness — Responses to grammatical errors in the Qur'an

cases.rationale: Graded contested because the Muslim defenses have real substance: several constructions do have parallels in pre-Islamic poetry and tribal dialects, grammar codification postdates the Quran, and the Uthman and Aisha reports carry disputed chains — this site will not lean on reports it would reject if they favored Islam. What survives the defenses is narrower but still notable: a book whose signature miracle is linguistic perfection contains a handful of constructions that required generations of harmonization, dialect appeals, and case-by-case special pleading — and the earliest Muslims transmitted reports alleging scribal error, which is not what a community certain of verbal perfection tends to preserve. Use this only with someone who cares about the i'jaz argument; it carries no weight with an ordinary Muslim friend and can look like pedantry. Christianity, note, claims inspired meaning through human authors (Luke 1:1-4), not dictated linguistic perfection — the comparison of claims, not texts, is the real point.

didyouknow.t: Islam's oldest monument is an anti-Trinitarian argument
didyouknow.d: The Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem (built 72 AH / 691-92 by caliph Abd al-Malik) carries the earliest monumental Islamic inscriptions in existence — and they are a direct polemic against Christian doctrine. The 240-meter mosaic band inside quotes and paraphrases Quran 4:171 and 19:35: 'Do not say Three... God is only one God; far be it from His glory that He should have a son.' Before Islam had minted its classic law books or collected its hadith, it was already defining itself against the Trinity — on Jerusalem's skyline, facing the Church of the Holy Sepulchre. The oldest physical Islamic proclamation is a denial of the Sonship of Christ.

didyouknow.t: The computer 'miracle' that ended in a murder
didyouknow.d: In the 1970s-80s, Egyptian-American biochemist Rashad Khalifa announced a computer-discovered 'mathematical miracle': the Quran's structure was built on the number 19 (from Quran 74:30). The catch: his counts only worked after he removed two verses (9:128-129) from the Quran as 'satanic insertions.' He went on to declare himself God's 'Messenger of the Covenant.' Mainstream scholars condemned him as an apostate, and on January 31, 1990 he was stabbed to death in his Tucson mosque; his killer was convicted in 2013. The episode is a case study in what happens when a 'proof' of the Quran requires editing the Quran — and in how heresy is policed.

didyouknow.t: Ashura: the wound that defines the Sunni-Shia split
didyouknow.d: Every year on 10 Muharram, Shia Muslims mourn the death of Husayn — Muhammad's grandson — killed with his family at Karbala (in modern Iraq) in 680 AD by the army of the caliph Yazid. Mourning processions include chest-beating, weeping majalis (lament gatherings), and in some communities self-flagellation with chains or blades (tatbir), though many Shia authorities now discourage blood rites and urge blood donation instead. Sunnis, by contrast, mark Ashura with an optional fast. That one day carries the whole Sunni-Shia divide in miniature: for Shia Islam, sacred history is a story of the Prophet's family betrayed by the Muslim community itself.

aboutyou.t: Sunni and Shia: a succession crisis at the very start
aboutyou.d: Islam split within a generation of Muhammad's death (632 AD) over who should lead: Abu Bakr, chosen by the community (the Sunni position), or Ali, Muhammad's cousin and son-in-law, designated by divine right (the Shia position). Karbala (680) sealed the divide in blood. Today roughly 85-90% of Muslims are Sunni and 10-15% Shia, concentrated in Iran, Iraq, Bahrain, Azerbaijan, and Lebanon. Twelver Shia — the large majority of Shia — hold that the twelfth imam, Muhammad al-Mahdi, entered hiding ('occultation') in 874 AD, is still alive, and will return as the Mahdi to bring justice.
aboutyou.tip: Never assume which tradition your friend belongs to — ask, and ask what it means to them; Shia friends especially may carry a strong sense of historical grievance and love for the Prophet's family. The split itself can open honest conversation: if God's final revelation left no clear successor and the community fractured immediately, what does that say about where authority really lies? Christians can point to a Shepherd who said his sheep hear his voice — and who never left.

aboutyou.t: Sufism: the mystical hunger inside Islam
aboutyou.d: Sufism is Islam's mystical stream — the whirling dervishes of the Mevlevi order (Rumi's heirs), dhikr chanting, saint veneration, and shrine pilgrimage. For centuries it was mainstream piety across much of the Muslim world, and it remains woven through South Asian, Turkish, and African Islam. Salafis and Wahhabis condemn shrine visitation and saint intercession as shirk (idolatry) — which is why jihadist and Salafi movements bulldoze Sufi shrines (Timbuktu 2012, ISIS across Iraq and Syria, the 2017 massacre of 300+ worshippers at a Sufi mosque in Sinai). The battle over Sufism is an intra-Islamic war about whether God can be intimately experienced.
aboutyou.tip: A Sufi-inclined friend is telling you something precious: they hunger for closeness to God, not just rule-keeping — and their own tradition's hardliners call that hunger idolatry. Don't debate; resonate. Share what union with God looks like in Christ: 'Abide in me' (John 15), the indwelling Spirit, adoption as sons. The longing Sufism reaches for through techniques and saints, the gospel offers as a gift and a certainty.

aboutyou.t: Hafiz culture: memorized sound vs. studied meaning
aboutyou.d: A hafiz is someone who has memorized the entire Quran in Arabic — all 6,000+ verses — and Muslim communities worldwide produce millions of them, often children. But since roughly 80% of Muslims are not native Arabic speakers, many huffaz can recite the whole book flawlessly without understanding the language. This isn't seen as a deficiency: in Islam the Quran IS the Arabic recitation — the sound itself is the sacred object, and reward attaches to recitation per letter. Translations are officially only 'interpretations of the meanings.' Christians relate to scripture almost oppositely: the Bible is meaning meant to be translated, studied, and understood, in every language from the start (Acts 2).
aboutyou.tip: Never belittle memorization — it reflects real devotion and discipline that puts most Christians' scripture engagement to shame; say so. Instead, ask meaning questions with genuine curiosity: 'That surah you recited — what is it saying? What does it mean to you?' Then offer to read a Gospel together in your friend's heart language. The experience of scripture that speaks directly, in their own tongue, about a God who wants to be understood, is often itself the door.
